analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal system for reporting illegal robocalls and lets phone companies offer free call-blocking.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and held a hearing, but never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The STOP Robocalls Act would require the Federal Communications Commission to set up a simpler way for individuals and companies to report illegal robocalls, spoofed caller ID, and illegal texts to the government. It would let phone and internet-calling companies provide a robocall-blocking service to customers free of charge, with customers able to turn it off if they want. It would also order the FCC to study whether internet-calling providers should have to keep contact and call records so unlawful calls can be traced back to their source. The bill never advanced past its House committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone rings with illegal robocalls or spoofed numbers. The bill would make it easier to report violations to the FCC, make free call-blocking widely available from phone companies, and build the record-keeping groundwork for tracing unlawful calls to their source.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to write rules creating a streamlined process for private parties to voluntarily share information about illegal robocalls, illegal texts, and caller-ID spoofing with the Commission.

Authorizes voice service providers to offer a robocall-blocking service to customers at no charge, with the customer able to opt out, while leaving providers free to offer opt-in blocking services with or without a fee.

Requires the FCC to study whether internet-calling (VoIP) providers should have to give the Commission current contact information and keep call records sufficient to trace any call back to its source, with a report to Congress within 18 months.

analysis.who_pays: Telecom and internet-calling companies would take on the cost of operating call-blocking services and, if the FCC later requires it, record-keeping and call-tracing data systems. Companies that profit from high-volume calling would face easier reporting of violations and better call tracing.

drawbacks.text: The information-sharing process is voluntary, and the call records provision is only a study, not a requirement — so the bill builds reporting channels and calls for further study rather than directly banning or penalizing more robocalls [S3].

The bill would cost voice service providers money to build and run blocking and record-keeping systems, and stricter call tracing raises the price of doing business for internet-calling providers, some of which serve low-cost call markets.
By its own terms the bill leaves the traceability requirements to a future FCC decision, so its main anti-robocall effect depends on later action the bill does not compel [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are real but modest: easier reporting of illegal calls and free call-blocking are conveniences and enforcement aids, not a reduction in robocalls by themselves. The costs fall on providers that would have to operate the systems, and the bill's centerpiece enforcement tool — call tracing through record retention — is deferred to a study rather than required. It is a groundwork bill: useful if follow-up rules are adopted, limited on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, which held a hearing, but no committee vote or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta introduced the bill on April 29, 2019, for himself and Rep. Michael F. Doyle of Pennsylvania, giving it support from both parties from the start.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and the subcommittee held hearings on it.
The bill drew 10 cosponsors — 3 Democrats and 7 Republicans — but never received a committee vote or a vote in the full House, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone and internet-calling companies avoided even the modest compliance obligations the bill contemplated, and high-volume illegal callers continued operating under the same rules that were in place before. Consumers gained nothing, since a bill that never reached a vote cannot lower the number of robocalls they receive.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured referral to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Michael F. Doyle
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 10 House cosponsors
for.role: 3 of 231 House Democrats and 7 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote, leaving it with the subcommittee after an initial hearing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — a Republican sponsor with a Democratic original cosponsor and cosponsors from both parties — so its death cannot be attributed to one party; it simply never reached a vote [S4].

industries.note: They would gain a clear legal basis to offer free call-blocking to customers, but would bear the cost of operating those services and, potentially, FCC-imposed contact and call-record requirements. Consumers get the blocking; the companies get the bill for it.

Easier reporting of violations and future call-tracing records would make it easier for regulators and phone companies to identify and block unlawful automated calls, the revenue source of this segment.
